newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU rejects French textile aid, but open to talks.
newsitem.headline: EU rejects French textile aid, but open to talks.

text.p: The European Commission said on Wednesday it had banned a French state aid scheme targeted at the textiles and clothing industries, but said it was open to discussions about a plan that would apply more widely.

EU Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert has invited French authorities to discuss ways of broadening or widening the system, for example to cover all sectors that are heavily dependent on manual labour.
The Commission "does not find fault with the plan's aims of job creation but rather with the fact that it supports certain sectors only," the European Union executive said in a statement.
Its decision means that some aid has to be repaid.
The Commission has consistently opposed sectoral aid, arguing that it distorts competition in the EU's border-free market.
Earlier this year it rejected an Italian plan to reduce social security payments for the country's footwear industry.
It cleared a Belgian scheme to cut social security charges on manual workers' wages in March after banning a previous scheme that gave tax breaks to export-led companies only.
There was a risk, it said, that the French plan would shift unemployment problems from one EU country to another.

The French plan, which has been allocated a budget of 2.1 billion French francs ($365.2 billion) per year for a period of 18 months, grants aid to employers in the form of cuts or exemptions in their social security contributions for low-paid workers.
In exchange, firms have undertaken to safeguard existing jobs and to create new jobs by hiring young unemployed people.
The Commission said the French plan did not create problems for some 11,300 of the 13,000 firms concerned since the benefits they received did not exceed minimum thresholds for state aid.
"On the other hand, the Commission's decision requires the aid to be recovered in cases where that threshold is exceeded," the Commission said.
Several technical meetings had taken place with French experts "which could logically be followed by a new concept that might be approved by the European Commission," it said.

The Commission warned in March that it was set to veto the plan because it took a sectoral approach rather than applying general measures to preserve jobs. But it delayed the final decision twice to give France time to make changes.
French Labour Minister Jacques Barrot said on Tuesday that he planned to extend the scheme and he hoped the Commission would at least offer another stay of execution on Wednesday.

Barrot told a news conference the aid had so far preserved 35,000 jobs, or half those that would have been lost in an industry plunged into difficulty by cheaper imports from rivals in countries whose currencies had fallen against the franc.
